links.title: Chapter 6: Lists - the lecture deck for this chapter
links.why: The slides this chapter is taught from, with the executed examples and the reader's notes for each slide. It sits in the chapter's own folder, one level above this page.

links.title: Chapter 6 - Lists, Automate the Boring Stuff with Python, 3rd Edition
links.why: The chapter this page renews, free to read online, with the Magic 8 Ball and Matrix screensaver programs.

links.title: 3. An Informal Introduction to Python (lists)
links.why: The tutorial's first account of lists, slices and the shallow copy made by the slice [:].

links.title: 5. Data Structures
links.why: Every list method, list comprehensions, del, tuples and the looping techniques, with enumerate.

links.title: Built-in Types (sequence types and mutable sequence types)
links.why: The operations that all sequences support, and those that only mutable sequences support, in two tables.

links.title: 3. Data model (objects, values and types)
links.why: The definition of identity, type and value behind the chapter's picture of names and references.

links.title: copy - Shallow and deep copy operations
links.why: The exact difference between copy.copy and copy.deepcopy, and how deepcopy handles a structure that contains itself.

links.title: random - Generate pseudo-random numbers
links.why: Reference for choice, shuffle and sample, with the notes on sequences.

links.title: Programming FAQ (multidimensional lists, shared default values)
links.why: The FAQ entries on creating a list of lists, on the tuple that raises an error while its list changes, and on default values that are shared.

links.title: Sorting Techniques
links.why: The key function, reverse and the stability of the sort, with worked examples.

links.title: Facts and myths about Python names and values
links.why: A short essay that explains with pictures why assignment copies references and what that means for lists and function arguments.

links.title: Timsort
links.why: The algorithm behind list.sort and sorted: its runs, its merging and its stability, created for Python by Tim Peters.

links.title: Fisher-Yates shuffle
links.why: The history of the fair shuffle from the pencil-and-paper method of 1938 to the computer version of 1964, and why naive shuffles are biased.

links.title: PEP 202 - List Comprehensions
links.why: The proposal that added list comprehensions to Python 2.0.

links.title: PEP 3132 - Extended Iterable Unpacking
links.why: The proposal for the starred name in an unpacking, as in first, *rest = seq.

links.title: PEP 448 - Additional Unpacking Generalizations
links.why: The proposal that allows [*a, *b] to spread several lists into one.

links.title: Why numbering should start at zero (EWD831)
links.why: The short note that argues for counting from zero and for half-open ranges, the convention of Python's index and slice.

links.title: Transforming Code into Beautiful, Idiomatic Python
links.source: Raymond Hettinger, PyCon US 2013 (YouTube, Next Day Video)
links.why: A core developer shows the idioms that replace index arithmetic: looping over a list, enumerate, unpacking and sorting with a key.

links.title: Facts and Myths about Python names and values
links.why: The talk behind the essay above: why two names can refer to one list and what a copy really copies.

links.title: Discussions on Python.org
links.why: The official forum where questions about the language are asked and answered.

links.title: Python Tutor
links.why: Run the aliasing, the function argument and the repeated list of lists step by step and watch the arrows from names to lists being drawn.
